title: Erdős Problem #1053: Growth Rate of k-Perfect Numbers
description: If σ(n) = k·n (n is k-perfect), must k = o(log log n)? Known: k = 11 exists. Gronwall: σ(n)/n = O(log log n). Robin's inequality gives k = O(log log n) conditionally on RH. Status: OPEN.

meta.author: Erdős, Guy (B2)

overview.historicalContext: The study of perfect numbers (sigma(n) = 2n) dates to Euclid's Elements (Book IX, Prop. 36), which proved that 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1) is perfect when 2^p - 1 is prime. Euler later proved the converse for even perfect numbers. The generalization to k-perfect numbers (sigma(n) = kn for k >= 3) was studied by the Renaissance mathematicians, with 120 recognized as the first triperfect number. In 1913, Gronwall proved the fundamental asymptotic result lim sup sigma(n)/(n log log n) = e^gamma, establishing that sigma(n)/n can grow like log log n. In 1984, Robin showed that sigma(n) < e^gamma * n * log log n for n >= 5041 assuming the Riemann Hypothesis, providing a conditional O(log log n) bound on k. Erdos asked the sharper question: must k = o(log log n)? Guy's Problem B2 in 'Unsolved Problems in Number Theory' conjectured the stronger statement that each k >= 3 has only finitely many k-perfect numbers. The largest known k is 11, and all known multiperfect numbers for k >= 3 are even.
overview.problemStatement: If n is k-perfect (sigma(n) = k * n), must k = o(log log n)? That is, for any epsilon > 0, is it true that k < epsilon * log log n for all sufficiently large k-perfect n? Status: OPEN. Robin's inequality gives the weaker k = O(log log n) conditionally on RH.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization axiomatizes the sum-of-divisors function sigma and defines IsKPerfect(n, k) as n > 0 and sigma(n) = k*n. Classical examples are stated for k = 1, 2, 3. Euler's characterization of even perfect numbers is axiomatized as an iff. The main conjecture (erdos_1053_conjecture) is formalized with epsilon-N quantifiers over k-perfect numbers. Gronwall's theorem and Robin's inequality are axiomatized, and their implication for k-perfect numbers (robin_gives_O_bound) is stated. Guy's stronger finiteness conjecture uses Set.Finite.
keyInsights: k = 2 (perfect numbers) have the Euclid-Euler characterization for even n; odd perfect numbers are unknown
Gronwall's theorem (1913) shows lim sup sigma(n)/(n log log n) = e^gamma ~ 1.781, so k = O(log log n) is the natural scale for k-perfect numbers
Robin's inequality (1984) gives k < e^gamma * log log n for k-perfect n >= 5041, conditional on RH; the question is whether the strict o() bound holds
Guy's finiteness conjecture (each k >= 3 has finitely many k-perfect numbers) is strictly stronger than Erdos's o(log log n) question
The largest known k is 11; all known multiperfect numbers (k >= 3) are even, suggesting deep structural constraints

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Axiomatizes sigma(n) as the sum-of-divisors function with sigma_def linking to Nat.divisors.sum. Defines IsKPerfect(n, k) requiring n > 0 and sigma(n) = k*n. Defines perfectMultiplicity(n) = sigma(n)/n as the integer ratio.

sections.title: Classical Perfect Numbers (k = 2)
sections.summary: States one_perfect_unique (only n=1 has sigma(n) = n), perfect_examples (6, 28, 496, 8128 are 2-perfect), and euler_even_perfect (even perfect numbers are exactly 2^{p-1}(2^p-1) for Mersenne primes 2^p-1).

sections.title: Multiperfect Numbers (k >= 3)
sections.summary: States triperfect_examples (120, 672, 523776 are 3-perfect) and largest_known_k (a k=11 perfect number exists). Notes that only finitely many k-perfect numbers are known for each k >= 3.

sections.title: The Main Conjecture
sections.summary: States erdos_1053_conjecture: for any epsilon > 0, there exists N such that for all k-perfect n >= N, k < epsilon * log(log(n)). This formalizes the o(log log n) growth constraint using epsilon-N quantifiers.

sections.title: Known Upper Bounds
sections.summary: Axiomatizes gronwall_bound (sigma(n) <= (1+epsilon) * e^gamma * n * log log n for large n) and robin_inequality_conditional (sigma(n) < e^gamma * n * log log n for n >= 5041, conditional on RH).

sections.title: Guy's Finiteness Conjecture
sections.summary: States guy_finiteness_conjecture: for each k >= 3, the set {n : IsKPerfect n k} is finite. This is strictly stronger than Erdos's o(log log n) question.

sections.title: Relationship to Robin's Criterion
sections.summary: States robin_gives_O_bound: if n >= 5041 and sigma(n) = k*n, then k < e^gamma * log log n. This gives k = O(log log n) conditional on RH; the Erdos question asks for the stronger o(log log n).

conclusion.summary: Erdos Problem #1053 asks whether k-perfect numbers must satisfy k = o(log log n). The formalization axiomatizes sigma, defines k-perfect numbers, states Euler's characterization of even perfect numbers, and presents both Gronwall's asymptotic bound and Robin's conditional inequality. The main conjecture is formalized with epsilon-N quantifiers, alongside Guy's stronger finiteness conjecture.
conclusion.implications: A resolution would illuminate the extremal behavior of the sum-of-divisors function and the structure of highly composite numbers. The connection to Robin's inequality means progress on the o() vs O() gap could relate to the Riemann Hypothesis. Guy's finiteness conjecture, if true, would imply that the sequence of k-perfect numbers terminates for each k, a strong structural constraint on multiplicative number theory.
openQuestions: Must k = o(log log n) for k-perfect numbers? (the central question of Problem #1053)
Are there only finitely many k-perfect numbers for each k >= 3? (Guy's stronger conjecture)
Does a k=12 perfect number exist, and if so, how large is it?
Do odd perfect numbers exist? (one of the oldest open problems in mathematics)
